content:
With so many supplements marketed for joint health, it can be hard to know what's worth trying. This evidence-based guide reviews the most popular arthritis supplements available in the UK, based on clinical research and expert opinion.

Quick answer: Omega-3 fish oil and turmeric have the most research behind them, but benefits are modest and vary, and high-dose omega-3 used in rheumatoid arthritis trials is not right for everyone. NICE does not recommend glucosamine for osteoarthritis. Always check with a GP or pharmacist before starting any supplement, especially if you take other medicines.

Can a supplement replace arthritis medication?

No supplement can cure arthritis or replace prescribed medication. Always consult your GP or pharmacist before starting any supplement, especially if you take blood thinners, diabetes medication, or other regular medicines.

Which supplements have the most research for arthritis?

1. Omega-3 Fish Oil

Evidence: some support in rheumatoid arthritis; modest and not consistent

  • Some trials in rheumatoid arthritis reported less joint pain and stiffness, but results vary
  • Trials used high doses (around 2-3g EPA/DHA daily). Check with your GP or pharmacist before taking high-dose fish oil, especially if you take blood thinners
  • UK brands: Seven Seas, Holland & Barrett, Boots own brand
  • Cost: approximately £8-15 per month

2. Turmeric / Curcumin

Evidence: Mixed to moderate for pain relief

  • Some small trials in knee osteoarthritis reported pain relief, but the evidence is mixed
  • Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.
  • Choose a supplement with piperine (black pepper extract) for better absorption
  • UK brands: Pukka, Together Health, Bio-Curcumin
  • Cost: approximately £10-20 per month

3. Vitamin D

NHS advice: supports bone and muscle health; not a treatment for arthritis

  • The NHS says that between October and early March we do not make enough vitamin D from sunlight, so everyone should consider 10 micrograms a day in autumn and winter
  • Low vitamin D has been linked with arthritis pain in some studies, but taking it has not been shown to treat arthritis
  • Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.
  • Available from any pharmacy or supermarket
  • Cost: approximately £3-8 per month

Which arthritis supplements have mixed or limited evidence?

4. Glucosamine and Chondroitin

Evidence: Mixed

  • NICE guideline NG226 says glucosamine should not be offered to manage osteoarthritis, because there is no strong evidence of benefit
  • Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.
  • Not suitable if you have a shellfish allergy (most glucosamine is shellfish-derived)

5. Collagen (Hydrolysed)

Evidence: Emerging but limited

  • Some studies suggest symptom improvement in OA
  • Evidence is preliminary; there is no good evidence that it repairs cartilage
  • UK brands: Vital Proteins, Great Lakes, Hunter & Gather

6. Ginger

Evidence: limited

  • Contains gingerols and shogaols with anti-inflammatory properties
  • Some small studies report modest benefit for OA pain; the evidence is limited
  • Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.
  • Generally safe; may interact with blood thinners

Where can you buy arthritis supplements in the UK?

  • Holland & Barrett — widest range of joint health supplements
  • Boots — pharmacist advice available in-store
  • Amazon UK — competitive prices, check seller ratings
  • Independent health food shops — often stock specialist brands

Always check for the MHRA "Traditional Herbal Registration" mark or GMP certification when buying supplements. Speak to your pharmacist about potential interactions with your current medications.

What should you do before trying a supplement?

If you are thinking about a supplement, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your primary care network about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Talking with your clinician

Bring the bottle or a photo to pharmacy or clinic appointments. Pharmacists can flag interactions with methotrexate, anticoagulants and other common arthritis medicines. Document start dates so you and your team can judge benefit honestly after several weeks.

Gentle cognitive tools

Noticing catastrophic thoughts ("this flare will never end") and reframing them with paced facts can reduce fear without denying real pain. Apps and courses based on cognitive behavioural approaches are available on the NHS in many areas; your surgery can advise what is offered locally.

Quick questions about arthritis supplements

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

Keep expectations kind while you try a supplement. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.

Frequently asked questions

Which supplements have the best evidence for arthritis?

Omega-3 (EPA/DHA) and some curcumin extracts have the strongest research for modest symptom relief in certain arthritis types. NICE does not recommend glucosamine for osteoarthritis, because there is no strong evidence of benefit. Benefits are usually small compared with prescribed treatments.

Do I need supplements if I already take arthritis medication?

Not necessarily. Supplements are optional add-ons, not replacements for DMARDs, biologics or physio. Check interactions with your pharmacist or clinician before starting anything new.

Is turmeric better than fish oil for joint pain?

They work differently and evidence varies by condition. Fish oil has more data in inflammatory arthritis; curcumin extracts are studied mainly in osteoarthritis. Neither is a cure, and product quality matters.

Are arthritis supplements safe to buy in the UK?

Choose reputable brands with clear dosing and third-party testing where possible. Watch for medicine interactions (for example blood thinners) and stop if you get side effects. Food supplements are not medicines.

How long before a supplement might help arthritis?

Trials that show benefit often run 8–12 weeks. If nothing changes after that period at a studied dose, continuing is unlikely to help. Keep a simple symptom note so you can judge fairly.

Should I take glucosamine and collagen together?

There is little reason to. NICE guideline NG226 says glucosamine should not be offered for osteoarthritis, and evidence for collagen is limited. Exercise and medical care come first; if you want to try a supplement, talk to a pharmacist and try one at a time rather than stacking products.
